The incident is the latest painful example of the aging US air traffic control telecom system and the ‌struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working. ... The first such interceptions by Bahraini air defences since September followed two warnings of potential threats, urging residents to seek shelter. US floated idea of Ukraine ceding ⁠Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskiy says US ​negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following ⁠the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi. This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles towards Riyadh, drones in Eastern Province The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province. The Houthis, who control most of the populous parts of Yemen, have intensified attacks on the Saudi capital in recent days. ... Top scorer on South Korean tax exam confesses to cheating with AI The marks attained by the top scorer on South Korea's national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true and on Sunday, sceptics were proven right when he confessed to using generative AI to cheat. The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea's high-stakes annual college entrance exam this Thursday. US air travel disruptions to persist until ​late on Sunday, FAA head says US air travel is not expected to return to normal schedules until late on Sunday, the head of the FAA said, as the aviation system gradually recovers from a nationwide flight shutdown that officials blamed on routine maintenance gone awry. As of 9:35 p.m. ET (0235 GMT), airlines on Saturday had canceled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000, according to FlightAware, an aviation website. That followed about 9,200 flights canceled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after ⁠the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already canceled. Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Canary Islands in one day Almost 1,500 migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands on Saturday, the highest number in a single day since 2020, the EFE news agency reported on Sunday, citing the maritime rescue service. A total of 1,488 people in 14 boats were rescued by the Spanish coastguard, EFE reported, continuing a surge of arrivals from West African countries to the Spanish archipelago since October.

items.title: Fed 'has some work to do on inflation,' Kansas City Fed chief says
items.excerpt: The Federal Reserve has the tools and responsibility to address price pressures that are "running too hot," and the central bank "has some work to do on inflation," Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said Sunday. Schmid, speaking to a credit union conference in Hawaii, did not specifically call for additional rate hikes, but said inflation is "uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target, and moving in the wrong direction." Common narratives that have recently evolved around the nature of current inflation and the Fed's ability to contain it are off-base, Schmid said. First, Schmid said, the view that high inflation is a reflection of repeated supply shocks neglects that "inflation is always the result of an imbalance between supply and demand. It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation." Schmid, who is not a Federal Open Market Committee voting member this year, said he also disagrees with the narrative that the sources of demand-induced inflation right now — like the artificial intelligence buildout — are resistant to Fed policy. The Fed raised rates by a quarter-percentage point in September to 3.75%-4.00% but opted not to lift them again at last month's meeting. After recent inflation readings came in higher than expected and comments from other Fed officials, including influential Governor Christopher Waller, interest rate futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point increase at December's meeting, with a small probability of a half-point hike. "I would also push back on the idea that meeting our inflation objective requires a reaction from any particular set of prices, for example prices for AI-related technology goods," Schmid said. "Both narratives — that inflation is being driven by either supply shocks or by demand that is impervious to higher interest rates — have a common core," Schmid said. "Mainly, that inflation is somehow beyond the Fed's power to control. I don't believe this to be true. The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability. As Chairman (Kevin) Warsh said, we have work to do." ## Fed's Collins: ... On Saturday, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said she supported a steady pace of modest interest rate increases because that path of action better manages economic uncertainties. When it comes to moving monetary policy to a tighter footing, "a steady, gradual path seems appropriate to me at the moment. But I'm open-minded," Collins told reporters at a conference held by her bank on housing issues in Boston. "I do see the risks as two-sided on the real side of the economy," Collins said, with inflation high and gains broadening throughout the economy, while the job market was stable and could accelerate. At the same time, Collins said, there are ongoing risks of more shocks hitting the economy. Furthermore, "it's possible that the rise in medium to longer term rates that we've seen since the beginning of the year may actually weigh on demand more than I'm thinking," and serve as another source of restraint on economic activity, she said. For now, all of that argues against the Fed shifting to a more aggressive pace of rate rises to contain inflation that has overshot the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, Collins said. Collins cautioned that her expectation that the Fed can move gradually "doesn't necessarily mean a particular cadence." She also reiterated that the data flow from recent months has shifted, where the Fed could end up in its current tightening cycle. "I do think that the price data we've seen over the past three months — and the labor market on a stronger footing — does make me think that the path of policy rates over the, you know, next year might be a bit higher than I had thought a couple of months ago," Collins said.

items.title: US consumer prices increase strongly for third straight month - Business Recorder
items.excerpt: Published November 15, 2026 Updated November 15, 2026 02:35am By Reuters WASHINGTON: US consumer prices increased more than expected in October, driven by higher costs for food and accommodation, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for the third straight month. The Labor Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Annual consumer inflation jumped 3.7 percent in September. Inflation is running well above the US central bank’s 2 percent target. The US-Israeli war with Iran has boosted oil prices, combining with the import tariffs implemented by the Trump administration last year to lift the cost of living. High inflation contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections last week. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that “a stronger policy move may be needed.” Waller also raised the prospect of a 50 basis point hike if core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, increased 0.3 percent or more from September, which they did. “Consumers’ inflation nightmare continues with no relief in sight,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “Fed officials are going to need to bring a bigger hose if they have any hope of putting the inflation fire out.” The CPI increased 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September. It was the third consecutive month of CPI gains of 0.4 percent or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI climbing 0.3 percent over the month. Shelter, which includes rents, hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30 percent of the increase in the CPI last month. Shelter costs rose 0.3 percent after climbing 0.4 percent in September. Food prices surged 0.5 percent after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices rebounded 0.4 percent, boosted by a 0.9 percent jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6 percent while fruits and vegetables were 0.6 percent more expensive. Prices for dairy and related products rose 0.6 percent. The cost of snacks surged 1.0 percent. Higher prices at the supermarket could be a reflection of more expensive diesel fuel. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home surging 0.5 percent after rising 0.2 percent in September. The cost of full service meals increased 0.7 percent. Gasoline prices climbed 1.0 percent after soaring 9.1 percent. Though diesel prices have come down from record highs, they rose 2.7 percent last month after increasing 11.9 percent in September. STRONG CORE INFLATION Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI increased 0.3 percent in October, advancing by the same margin for three months in a row. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2 percent in October. Core CPI inflation increased 2.6 percent year-over-year in September. It was last month driven by a 0.3 percent rise in owners’ equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property. Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6 percent. Airline fares rose 0.4 percent. The cost of recreation increased 0.8 percent, while motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7 percent. Household furnishings and supplies prices rebounded 0.7 percent, suggesting that some pass-through from tariffs remained. There were also increases in the prices of new vehicles, medication and recreation goods.

items.title: Inflation will be key to future interest rate decisions: US Fed official
items.excerpt: San Diego [US], November 15: US Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip N Jefferson has said that inflation will be the key factor in determining future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain elevated despite signs of stability in the American economy and labour market. Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said, "Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy." He added, "Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks." Jefferson's remarks come as US inflation continues to remain well above the Federal Reserve's 2 per cent target. According to the data cited in his speech, the annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation rate stood at 3.6 per cent in September, while core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, was 3.1 per cent. Expressing concern over persistent price pressures, Jefferson said, "I remain concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly." He noted that higher energy costs were affecting sectors such as airfares and transportation, while strong demand for new technologies was also pushing up prices of certain goods, including memory chips. Jefferson said inflation data received so far for October remained consistent with price pressures staying well above the Fed's target. On the labour market, he said conditions had stabilised, with the unemployment rate standing at 4.1 per cent in October. "I expect the unemployment rate to stay around its current level in the near term-a level I view as consistent with maximum employment," he said. Jefferson also noted that the US economy had gained momentum this year, with gross domestic product (GDP) expanding at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent in the third quarter. "The economy has gained momentum this year, expanding at a pace roughly in line with its potential," he said.

items.title: Trump’s judge appointment blitz faces Republican resistance By Reuters
items.excerpt: By David Morgan and Nate Raymond WASHINGTON, Nov 15 (Reuters) - A last-minute effort by US President Donald Trump to install as many judges as possible before Democrats take control of the US Senate is running into resistance from some fellow Republicans. Until recently, Senate Republicans had routinely approved Trump’s nominees for lifetime seats on district and appeals courts during his second term, confirming 57 so far and helping him cement a conservative imprint on the judiciary that will outlast his presidency. But as the White House and Senate Republican leaders press ahead with judicial nominees during the lame-duck session, a handful of Republicans have blocked or cast doubt on three nominees selected for their home states. Senators traditionally help choose judges for vacancies in their states. Trial court nominees are especially vulnerable because, under Senate custom, home-state senators can block them by withholding a “blue slip," a form indicating support to the Senate Judiciary Committee. While generally honoring that tradition, the White House has sometimes picked conservatives to fill judicial vacancies over the objections of Republican senators. "We put up a lot of really qualified candidates that we sent to the White House, and they basically ignored that and just put through their one," Senator Alan Armstrong, an Oklahoma Republican, said. Two outgoing Republican members on the Senate Judiciary Committee, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, can deny such nominees the votes needed to advance. ’NOT THE WAY IT WORKS HERE’ The White House on Tuesday took the rare step of withdrawing US District Judge Lee Rudofsky’s nomination to the St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals and replacing him with Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland after US Senators John Boozman and Tom Cotton of Arkansas opposed Rudofsky. Outgoing Republican Senators Armstrong and Cornyn have withheld public support for two nominees in their states, while Tillis has used his position on the committee to help block candidates opposed by his colleagues. Tillis, who has a fractured relationship with Trump, told reporters on Thursday that the White House has at times essentially told senators, "This is our guy, I hope you’ll get on board." "That’s not how it works here," he said. "They should expect they’re going to get this response." For the White House, the next few weeks reflect the last hurrah on a project that began during Trump’s first administration to shift the federal judiciary’s ideological balance to the right, an initiative whose effects will be felt for years after Trump leaves office. "We expect all judicial nominees pending in the Senate to be confirmed this year," a White House official said in a statement. Trump made 234 judicial appointments during his first term in office from 2017 to 2021, including three members of the US Supreme Court’s current 6-3 conservative supermajority. Roughly one-third of active judges are now Trump appointees. THUNE PRIORITIZING JUDICIAL NOMINATIONS Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Monday that judicial confirmations were a top priority while Republicans retain control of the chamber. The Senate confirmed its first judicial nominee of the lame-duck session on Thursday. Twenty-three nominees remain pending, including Colorado-based US District Judge Daniel Domenico, whose nomination to the Denver-based 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals is set for a Monday vote. But Tillis, who is retiring, and Cornyn, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, are now in their final days in office and have indicated a willingness to block some nominees pending before the Senate Judiciary Committee, of which they are both members. Rob Luther, a George Mason University law professor who worked on judicial nominations in the White House Counsel’s Office during Trump’s first term, said senators who are now on "borrowed time" stand in the way of "movement conservatives" being appointed to the bench.

items.title: Johnny Depp film ‘Ebenezer’ gets actor first No. 1 opening in 8 years
items.excerpt: Nov. 15, 2026, 1:20 PM EST By The Associated Press Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with his first studio movie in eight years, and since fallout from a contentious libel trial against ex-wife Amber Heard left his future in Hollywood in jeopardy. But six years after he was asked to leave the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise, and three years after Depp said that he had “no further need for Hollywood,” “Ebenezer,” a Paramount Pictures release, opened in first place with about $19 million in ticket sales, according to studio estimates on Sunday. Paramount released it in 3,535 theaters. While it might be a far cry from the heights of the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, which twice opened over $100 million, or even the $62 million opening of “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald” in 2018, it is a solid start for the film, which cost a reported $38 million to produce. Internationally, it made $23 million from 63 markets, adding up to a $42 million global debut. Outside of his franchise fare, Depp more often had openings in the $20 million range (as with “Black Mass” and “Public Enemies”). The audience for “Ebenezer” was about 52% female and 81% over the age of 25, according to PostTrak exit polls. About 65% of ticket buyers said they would “definitely” recommend the film to friends. Less than half, or 47%, of the “kid” demographic (ages 12 and under) said they would tell their friends they “must see it right away.” The Charles Dickens-inspired tale is rated PG-13 and directed by Ti West, who is best known for the horror franchise X. Critics were not as warm as audiences about the film. It’s currently sitting at 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley also star. ... Sony’s “Ghost Soldier” and Amazon MGM Studios’ “How to Rob a Bank” also opened this weekend to less fanfare. “Ghost Soldier,” an action film starring Jim Caviezel, debuted in sixth place with $5.2 million from 2,558 theaters. “How to Rob a Bank” landed in seventh place with just under $5.2 million from 2,810 theaters. Internationally, it made $5.1 million. The film from “The Fall Guy” director David Leitch had a reported net production budget of $40 million. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, “How to Rob a Bank” did not receive good reviews. ... “The Cat in the Hat” landed in second place in its second weekend in theaters with $11.4 million, followed by “Godzilla Minus Zero” in third place with $8.3 million (down a whopping 73% from its opening). Fourth place went to “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” also in its second weekend, with $5.5 million. And the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” rounded out the top five with just under $5.5 million, bringing its domestic total to $89 million. “Wild Horse Nine” also added 1,075 theaters in its second weekend, where it earned $4.6 million. Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” had one of the best limited expansions of the year with $756,060 on 27 screens. And James Gray’s acclaimed crime thriller “Paper Tiger” opened in six locations in New York and Los Angeles to $215,009 before it expands nationwide next week. Overall it was a slower weekend than last with around $86 million in total ticket sales from North American theaters.

items.excerpt: Phil Collins cries, Billy Idol shouts and rappers romp at Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony has been a lively celebration. Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech, while Cynthia Erivo delivered an electrifying tribute. Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan brought a rowdy celebration to the stage. Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte, Sade, Joy Division/New Order, and Iron Maiden were also inducted. U2 surprised the audience by opening the night, and Run DMC and Aerosmith closed with a loud jam. Despite some absences, the event was vibrant and memorable, with performances and tributes that kept the crowd engaged. ... Glenn Close and Ridley Scott to get honorary Oscars at Governors Awards LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close will finally hold an Oscar and make an acceptance speech after eight nominations without a win. She will receive an honorary Academy Award for her five-decade career at the Governors Awards on Sunday night. Director Ridley Scott of films like “Alien” and “Gladiator” will also receive an honorary Oscar. He plans to accept via recorded video. Disney animator Floyd Norman and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will be honored too. Close shares the record with Peter O’Toole for the most nominations without a win. She has won other major awards throughout her long career, ... A look at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame 2026 inductees and how they were honored LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical legends at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Phil Collins enters again for his solo career, inducted by Travis Barker. Wu-Tang Clan, inducted by Chris Rock, performed a medley of hits. Queen Latifah, inducted by Megan Thee Stallion, received the Early Influence Award. Luther Vandross was honored by Oprah Winfrey, with Usher performing his songs. Rick Rubin, inducted by Neil Young, received the Musical Excellence Award. Other inductees include Iron Maiden, Oasis, Joy Division, and New Order, among others. Richard Sterban, member of the celebrated country and gospel group The Oak Ridge Boys, dies at 83 Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, has died. He was 83. His family and the band say he died Saturday in Hendersonville, Tennessee, due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after a long battle with cancer. Sterban was a native of New Jersey. He left his job as a backup singer for Elvis Presley to join the vocal group, best known perhaps for its rendition of “Elvira.” The band won five Grammy awards, and its members were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015. In 2011 they gained membership in the Grand Ole Opry.
